---
title: "Link functions"
---

The [preceding page](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd) showed why binary probabilities and positive expected counts cannot be represented by an unconstrained straight-line mean. The [design-matrix page](design-matrices.qmd) already introduced the real-valued linear predictor:

$$
\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.
$$

A conditional mean may be constrained. A Bernoulli mean must lie between zero and one, and a Poisson mean must be positive. A [**link function**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) connects these two scales.

The link function performs this mapping between the conditional mean and the real-valued linear predictor. The linear predictor remains
free to take any real value, while the inverse link guarantees that the resulting
conditional mean lies in the range licensed by the response measurement.

## Link and inverse link

Let

$$
\mu_i=\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid x_i].
$$

The link function $g$ maps the mean to the linear predictor:

$$
g(\mu_i)=\eta_i.
$$

The inverse link maps back:

$$
\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i).
$$

The two directions answer different computational questions. The link asks,
"Which unconstrained value represents this conditional mean?" The inverse link
asks, "Which conditional mean corresponds to this unconstrained value?"

Regression predictions usually travel in the second direction. Predictors and
coefficients produce $\eta_i$, then the inverse link produces $\mu_i$.

For ordinary linear regression, the identity link gives $g(\mu)=\mu$. For logistic regression, the logit link gives

$$
g(\pi)=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}.
$$

For Poisson regression, the log link gives

$$
g(\lambda)=\log\lambda.
$$

Its inverse is

$$
g^{-1}(\eta)=e^\eta.
$$

Exponentiation maps every real value to a positive value. It can produce a
conditional mean below 1, such as $.3$, even though an observed count must be an
integer. A distributional mean need not itself be an observable response.

For a Bernoulli response, the inverse logit is

$$
g^{-1}(\eta)
=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}.
$$

This function maps the real line into $(0,1)$. At $\eta=0$, it gives probability
$.5$. Large positive values approach 1, and large negative values approach 0.

## Constructing a mapping table

```{r}
#| label: compare-inverse-link-ranges
#| echo: true
eta <- c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)

data.frame(
  eta = eta,
  identity_mean = eta,
  logit_mean = plogis(eta),
  log_mean = exp(eta)
)
```

The identity inverse link reproduces the real-valued predictor. The inverse
logit stays between zero and one. The exponential remains positive. The same
linear-predictor values thus imply different mean scales under different MRMs.

## Coefficients live on the link scale

If $x$ increases by one, $\eta$ changes by $\beta_1$. This is an additive statement on the link scale.

Under a log link,

$$
\lambda(x+1)
=
\exp(\eta+\beta_1)
=
\lambda(x)\exp(\beta_1).
$$

The response mean is multiplied by $\exp(\beta_1)$. Under a logit link, $\exp(\beta_1)$ instead multiplies the odds.

The response-mean difference is not generally constant. Under the inverse
logit, adding 1 to $\eta$ changes probability from $.50$ to about $.731$ when
$\eta$ starts at 0. The same addition changes probability from about $.881$ to
$.953$ when $\eta$ starts at 2. The link-scale change is 1 in both cases, while
the probability changes are about $.231$ and $.072$.

A constant coefficient on the link scale does not generally produce a constant difference on the response scale. Nonlinear inverse links make the response-scale difference depend on the other predictor values.

## Verifying the two directions

For a Bernoulli mean $\pi=.8$, the logit link gives

$$
\eta
=\log\frac{.8}{1-.8}
=\log4
\approx1.386.
$$

Applying the inverse returns

$$
\frac{1}{1+e^{-1.386}}\approx.8.
$$

For a count mean $\lambda=5$, the log link gives $\eta=\log5$. Exponentiating
returns 5. These round trips are useful checks on a coefficient interpretation.

## Keeping the link separate from the response family

The response family determines possible observations and a mean-variance
relation. The link determines how predictors change the conditional mean. These
are distinct model choices.

For instance, the Bernoulli family supplies responses 0 and 1. The logit link is
one way to keep their conditional probability valid. Another monotone mapping
could also stay within $(0,1)$ while implying a different relation between
$\eta$ and probability.

The fact that a mapping has the right range is necessary but not sufficient. Its
shape affects coefficient interpretation and extrapolation. The mapping should
be stated and its response-scale predictions checked.

## Comparing on the response scale

With a nonlinear inverse link, a constant change in $\eta$ does not produce a constant change in $\mu$. Report predicted probabilities or expected counts at meaningful predictor values. These response scale summaries are often easier to connect to a linguistic claim than a link scale coefficient alone.

A good report retains both scales. The coefficient gives the additive change in
$\eta$. A prediction table shows what that change means for probabilities or
expected counts at the predictor values relevant to the linguistic contrast.

family and a linear predictor.
